args.command: cat caravel_summary.md; head -5 caravel_ab.csv; wc -l caravel_ab.csv

cat caravel_ab.csv | tail -26; python3 -c "
import csv,math
r=list(csv.DictReader(open('caravel_ab.csv')))
t={}
for x in r:
  a=t.setdefault(x['variant'],[0,0]);a[0]+=int(x['visitors']);a[1]+=int(x['conversions'])
print(t)
(n1,c1),(n2,c2)=t['control'],t['new_checkout']
p1,p2=c1/n1,c2/n2;p=(c1+c2)/(n1+n2)
z=(p2-p1)/math.sqrt(p*(1-p)*(1/n1+1/n2));print(p1,p2,p2/p1-1,z,math.erfc(abs(z)/2**.5))"

outcomes.prose:
Show the working as a cell.

**The summary overstates the result. The data doesn't support signing off on the lift as written.**

The cell above computes it from `caravel_ab.csv`. I summed visitors and conversions per variant over all 14 days, then ran a pooled two-proportion z-test. I also checked the numbers in Python.

| | Control | New checkout |
|---|---|---|
| Conversions / visitors | 700 / 14,000 | 742 / 14,000 |
| Conversion rate | 5.00% | 5.30% |

- **The 12% is wrong:** the relative lift is 6.0% (0.30 percentage points). The summary's figure is about double that.
- **The p-value is wrong:** z ≈ 1.14, so two-sided p ≈ 0.26, not 0.004. That is not significant, and the 95% interval on the difference includes zero.
- **The direction is encouraging:** the new checkout is ahead on most days. A gap of 0.3 points on this much traffic is still well within noise.

I don't know where 12% and 0.004 came from. You could check the original analysis for a different data cut or a calculation error.

**Recommendation:** don't ship on Monday based on this test. If the team still wants an answer, keep running it. To detect a 6% relative lift at 5% baseline you'd need roughly 100k visitors per arm. That is about 3 months at the current traffic.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
**What it does:** `debounce(fn, wait)` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels the pending timer and starts a new `wait`-ms timer. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no further calls. It runs once, with the arguments from the last call.

Limits of this version:
- It is trailing-edge only. It never fires on the first call.
- It doesn't preserve `this`, because the wrapper is an arrow function.
- It has no `cancel` or `flush`.
- It discards `fn`'s return value.

**Debounce vs. throttle:**
- **Debounce:** use it when you only care about the final state after a burst of events. Examples are search-as-you-type requests, autosaving after the user stops editing, and validating a field. Another is recalculating layout once a window resize ends.
- **Throttle:** use it when you need regular updates *during* a continuous stream. Examples are scroll position tracking, drag or mousemove handlers, and progress reporting. It runs `fn` at most once per interval.

A continuous stream of events with gaps shorter than `wait` keeps a debounced function from ever firing. Throttle avoids that.

outcomes.prose:
HTTP 418 means **"I'm a teapot."** RFC 2324 defined it as an April Fools' joke, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP). A teapot returns it when it is asked to brew coffee, because it can't.

Real servers sometimes use it as an unofficial response. Some use it to refuse a request, for example to block bots. It isn't meant for normal use.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Design-language persona: developer, benchmark takeaway

components.text: ## simdjson-port wins at every size, and its lead grows with input

components.title: Takeaways
components.text: v2 is a steady ~2× over v1. serde-wasm is only slightly ahead of v2 and beats it just at 100 KB+. At 1 KB, differences are microseconds, likely noise or overhead. Check memory, binary size and correctness before choosing.

outcomes.prose:
**Main takeaway:** simdjson-port is fastest at every size. Its advantage grows with input: about 2.7× faster than v1 at 1 KB, 6.6× at 100 KB and 7.7× at 10 MB.

- **v2 vs v1:** v2 is a steady improvement of about 1.6–2×.
- **serde-wasm vs v2:** serde-wasm is only marginally faster than v2, and it is slower at 1 KB. It isn't a meaningful step up.
- **1 KB results:** the differences are tens of microseconds, so fixed overhead and noise probably dominate. Don't read much into the ranking there.
- **Caveats:** these are medians only. Before you commit to simdjson-port, check variance (p95), memory use, binary size and correctness on edge cases. Also check whether your real payloads are closer to 1 KB or 10 MB, since the gap matters most for large inputs.

components.text: ## You don't run out in any scenario (if $38k is expenses)

components.title: Assumption matters
components.text: If $38k is already net burn (after revenue), cash lasts 480/38 ≈ 12.6 months with no growth help, i.e. out around month 13 (Dec 2027).

outcomes.prose:
I treated $38k as monthly expenses, so net burn is $38k minus revenue. Revenue compounds from $12k.

- **5% growth:** cash bottoms out around $102k in month 24, then recovers. Revenue passes $38k at about month 24.
- **8% growth:** cash bottoms out around $236k in month 15.
- **12% growth:** cash bottoms out around $310k in month 11.

On this reading you never run out of money, even at 5%. At 5% the cushion is thin, so a small miss on growth or costs could change that.

If $38k is already net burn, revenue is already counted. Then you run out in about 12.6 months, which is around December 2027.

components.text: Meets SSO, longest retention, only self-host option, and $42/mo cheaper than Bugsnag. Rollbar's SSO is enterprise-only, so its list price understates the real cost.

outcomes.prose:
I'd pick **Sentry**, at about $364/month for 14 seats. The matrix above shows the comparison.

- **Honeybadger** is out because it has no SSO.
- **Rollbar** is out on the list prices you gave me. SSO is enterprise-only there, so $294/month isn't the real cost. You'd need a quote to know it.
- **Bugsnag** does have SSO, but it costs about $42/month more than Sentry. It also keeps data for 60 days instead of 90, and it can't be self-hosted.

Sentry is the cheaper of the two vendors that offer SSO at the listed price. It also has the longest retention and is the only one you can self-host. Check that its SSO is included in the $26 seat plan, because vendors sometimes limit SSO to higher tiers.
